title: Multiplying, Powers and De Moivre's Theorem
short: Multiply moduli and add angles; zⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).
trouble: Students multiply the angles instead of adding them.

blocks.html: Multiplying $a + bi$ by $c + di$ in rectangular form is a chore. In polar form it becomes almost trivial, and powers become easy. The reason is the sum formulas.

$$r_1(\cos\alpha + i\sin\alpha) \cdot r_2(\cos\beta + i\sin\beta) = r_1r_2\big(\cos(\alpha + \beta) + i\sin(\alpha + \beta)\big)$$ Multiply the moduli and add the angles; to divide, divide the moduli and subtract the angles. Repeating gives De Moivre's theorem: $$\big[r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\big]^n = r^n(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta).$$

Multiply out: $$(\cos\alpha + i\sin\alpha)(\cos\beta + i\sin\beta) = (\cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta) + i(\sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta),$$ using $i^2 = -1$. The real part is $\cos(\alpha + \beta)$ and the imaginary part is $\sin(\alpha + \beta)$. So multiplying by a complex number stretches by its modulus and rotates by its angle. Doing that $n$ times rotates $n$ times.

blocks.name: complexplane
blocks.cap: The product $zw$: its length is $|z||w|$ and its angle is the sum of the two angles.

blocks.html: Multiplying the angles instead of adding them, as in $\frac{\pi}{6} \cdot \frac{\pi}{3}$. Angles add because rotations combine: turn $30^\circ$, then $60^\circ$, and you have turned $90^\circ$. Only in a power, $z^n$, does the angle get multiplied, by the whole number $n$, because you add it $n$ times.
